summary: Extends the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) so it can carry Flow Specifications, as defined in RFC 8955. Flow Specifications describe traffic flows by matching on packet fields. With this extension, a path computation element can tie traffic flows to the paths it computes for them.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets a route planner say which kind of traffic should use which road.

questions: how to steer traffic with pce flowspec
what is a flow specification in pcep
subtitle: How a path computation server tells a router which traffic belongs on which tunnel, using the protocol it already speaks.

tldr.problem: A Path Computation Element (PCE) can set up and control tunnels such as LSPs and SR paths, but the head end of a tunnel still needs to be told what traffic to put on it, usually by separate manual configuration.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a FLOWSPEC object to PCEP that carries BGP-style Flow Specifications in a Flow Filter TLV, plus a capability TLV, an add/modify/remove procedure and a new set of error codes.
tldr.outcome: A PCE can create, update and withdraw traffic-to-tunnel mappings in the same messages that manage the tunnels. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 9168 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes paths for traffic engineering networks. It talks to Path Computation Clients (PCCs) using the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) from RFC 5440. With the stateful extensions of RFC 8231 and RFC 8281, a PCE can also initiate tunnels such as Label Switched Paths (LSPs) or Segment Routing (SR) paths.

Setting up a tunnel is only half the job. The head end also has to know what traffic to place on it. RFC 8955 describes traffic flows with Flow Specifications: matching criteria applied to IP packets, distributed in BGP. This RFC reuses that idea inside PCEP, so the same protocol that sets up the tunnel can say what goes onto it.

There is one difference from BGP. No action is carried, because the only action that makes sense in PCEP is to direct matching traffic onto the identified tunnel. The Flow Specifications are meant to be installed only at the head end of the LSP they feed.
sections.plainLanguage: Building a road is not enough. Someone has to say which cars use it. This RFC lets the route planner say that in the same message it uses to build the road.

sections.title: Where Flow Specifications Fit in PCE Procedures
sections.content:
The RFC lists five steps in setting up and using an LSP: decide which LSPs to set up, decide their properties, decide what traffic to put on them, cause them to be set up, and tell the head end what traffic to put on the LSP. Only the last step is the subject of this document.

Three elements make it work. Peers must be able to say whether they support Flow Specifications. A PCE or PCC must be able to include them in PCEP messages with clear rules about applicability and overlap. And the state must be synchronized between peers so that, after a recovery, both sides agree on which Flow Specifications apply.

The FLOWSPEC object is optional and may appear more than once in PCInitiate, PCUpd, PCRpt, PCReq, PCRep and PCErr messages. An active PCE uses PCInitiate and PCUpd to say what traffic a path should carry. A PCC uses PCRpt to report what it places on a path, and can use PCReq to hint at the purpose of a tunnel it is asking for. As with other path attributes, a PCC applies its local policy to what it receives.

Flow Specifications travel with LSP state, so they become part of the LSP database and are synchronized with it, using the procedures of RFC 8231 or the enhanced ones of RFC 8232.
sections.plainLanguage: The planner can pass notes about which traffic belongs on a path in many of the messages it already sends. If a note gets lost, both sides compare notes again so they agree.

sections.title: Advertising and Negotiating the Capability
sections.content:
A PCE or PCC that supports this extension includes the PCE-FLOWSPEC-CAPABILITY TLV in the OPEN object of its PCEP Open message. The TLV has type 51 and a fixed length of 2 octets. Its value must be 0 and is ignored on receipt, followed by two bytes of zero padding.

If either peer leaves the TLV out, the other peer MUST NOT send a FLOWSPEC object. If one arrives anyway, the receiver replies with a PCErr: Unknown Object if it does not support this specification, or Not supported object if it does but has not enabled it on that session.

Support can also be advertised in IGP discovery. This RFC defines bit 16, the FlowSpec Capable flag, in the PCE-CAP-FLAGS sub-TLV. That advertisement is only a hint: peers that want to use Flow Specifications MUST still negotiate during PCEP session setup, and a peer that advertised support in the IGP is not obliged to support it on every session.
sections.plainLanguage: Before passing traffic notes, each side says at the door whether it understands them. If it did not say so, nobody sends it any.

sections.title: The FLOWSPEC Object
sections.content:
The FLOWSPEC object has Object-Class 43 and Object-Type 1. Each instance describes one traffic flow. Its body has four fixed fields followed by TLVs.

  • FS-ID (32 bits) identifies the Flow Specification. It is unique within the PCE or PCC that originates it and constant for the PCEP session. The values 0 and 0xFFFFFFFF are reserved.
  • AFI (16 bits) is the BGP address family: 1 for IPv4 or VPNv4, 2 for IPv6 or VPNv6.
  • Flags (8 bits) define two bits. The R (Remove) bit asks to remove the Flow Specification instead of adding or modifying it. The L (Longest Prefix Match) bit asks for the filter to be installed as a route subject to LPM forwarding rather than as a Flow Specification policy.

Two TLVs may appear. The SPEAKER-ENTITY-ID TLV from RFC 8232 is mandatory, and together with the FS-ID it uniquely identifies the Flow Specification. The Flow Filter TLV carries the actual match rule. It must be present when R is clear and is optional when R is set.

If L is set, only Flow Specifications describing IPv4 or IPv6 destinations are meaningful. A receiver that cannot install them as an LPM route replies with Error-Type 30, Error-value 5. Filtering based on Layer 2 fields is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a ticket number, says whether it is about IPv4 or IPv6, and has a switch for add or cancel. The details of which traffic it means go in an attached card.

sections.title: Flow Filter and Flow Specification TLVs
sections.content:
The Flow Filter TLV (type 52) holds one or more Flow Specification TLVs, which together define one flow. A FLOWSPEC object can carry only one Flow Filter TLV; further flows go in further objects.

Flow Specification TLV types come from their own IANA registry. Types 0 to 255 mirror the BGP Flow Spec registries of RFC 8955 (IPv4) and RFC 8956 (IPv6, chosen by the AFI). BGP uses one octet for the type while PCEP uses two, so the range 256 to 65535 is left for new PCEP-specific types. Values for types 0 to 255 reuse the BGP encoding without the type octet and are zero-padded to 4-byte alignment.

Multiple TLVs in one filter are combined into a more detailed match. A filter MUST NOT contain two TLVs of the same type, and a receiver that sees that replies with a Malformed FlowSpec error and does not install it. An unrecognized type gets an Unsupported FlowSpec error. For example, a flow for a source and destination IPv6 pair is the combination of a Destination IPv6 Prefix TLV and a Source IPv6 Prefix TLV.

The RFC defines three new types: 256 (Route Distinguisher), 257 (IPv4 Multicast Flow) and 258 (IPv6 Multicast Flow). The Route Distinguisher TLV carries an 8-octet value in the format of RFC 4364, which lets a flow be tied to a VPN. The tunnel head end then recognizes that VPN's traffic by its usual means, such as the incoming port or the VRF, rather than by packet fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The attached card is built from small pieces such as destination, source or VPN name. Putting several pieces together narrows down which traffic you mean, but you cannot use the same kind of piece twice.

sections.title: Modifying, Removing and Prioritizing Flows
sections.content:
To modify a Flow Specification, the sender includes all the TLVs for the new definition, keeps the same FS-ID and uses the same Speaker Entity Identifier. To add one, it sends a new FS-ID with R clear. Each flow normally gets its own FLOWSPEC object, and several objects can sit in one message or be spread across messages.

To remove one, the sender sends an object with the matching FS-ID and R set. No TLVs are needed. If TLVs are present, the receiver may ignore them, and if they do not match what is recorded, the flow is still removed and the receiver SHOULD log it. Removing an unknown FS-ID yields Error-value 4 (Unknown FlowSpec).

Flow Specifications can overlap, so the PCC needs a predictable order. PCCs MUST apply the ordering rules of RFC 8955, including when the same implementation also receives Flow Specifications through BGP. An implementation may offer a setting that lets one protocol win over the other, and logging a message when the two overlap is RECOMMENDED. If a new Flow Specification cannot be resolved against those installed, the receiver replies with Error-value 3 (Unresolvable Conflict) and does not install it.

By default no Flow Specification applies to a tunnel. How head ends learn what to put on tunnels is then a local matter, such as configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: To change a note, you send a new one with the same ticket number. To cancel, you send the number with the cancel switch. If two notes fight over the same cars, a fixed rule decides who wins.

sections.title: Error Codes and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
This RFC defines PCEP Error-Type 30, FlowSpec Error, with five error values used throughout the procedures above. IANA also assigned Object-Class 43, TLV types 51 and 52, a new registry for the object's flag bits (bit 6 is L and bit 7 is R, counting from bit 0 as the most significant), a registry for Flow Specification TLV types, and bit 16 in the OSPF PCE Capability Flags registry.

The new Flow Specification TLV registry reserves 0 to 255 and uses Specification Required for 256 to 64506, First Come First Served for 64507 to 65531, and Experimental Use for 65532 to 65535.
sections.plainLanguage: When something is wrong with a note, the receiver sends back a numbered complaint so the sender knows exactly what to fix.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
Systems that use a remote PCE are already exposed to spurious or modified paths. Flow Specifications add another target: an attacker can misroute traffic without tearing down any tunnel. The RFC therefore points to the existing PCEP protections and says deployments concerned with privacy MUST secure the session with IPsec (RFC 5440) or TLS (RFC 8253). TCP-MD5 is described as insufficient and SHOULD NOT be relied upon.

It also warns that overlapping Flow Specifications installed in different orders can give unexpected results, which could open gaps in monitoring or let traffic avoid expected mitigations.

For operators, a PCC MUST let an operator view installed Flow Specifications in order of precedence, so that the one served first is shown first. Implementations MAY offer a switch to enable or disable the feature, and a PCE SHOULD allow per-PCC variations in precedence ordering. The RFC says the feature makes no direct change to how the network operates, since traffic is already placed on paths by some configuration mechanism. Instead it reduces the number of mechanisms that must be used.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad guy could change the notes, cars would be sent down the wrong road. So the messages must be locked, and the person running the network must be able to see the list in order.

fields.name: FS-ID
fields.desc: Identifier of the Flow Specification; 0 and 0xFFFFFFFF are reserved.

fields.name: AFI
fields.desc: 1 for IPv4 or VPNv4, 2 for IPv6 or VPNv6.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on transmission, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Includes the L (LPM) bit and the R (Remove) bit; unassigned bits are zero.

items.label: Unsupported FlowSpec
items.desc: A Flow Specification TLV type is not recognized or supported.

items.label: Malformed FlowSpec
items.desc: Duplicate TLV types, a missing Speaker Entity ID or Flow Filter TLV, an unsupported AFI, or G set without S.

items.label: Unresolvable Conflict
items.desc: The new Flow Specification cannot be resolved against installed ones.

items.label: Unknown FlowSpec
items.desc: Remove requested for an FS-ID that does not exist.

items.label: Unsupported LPM Route
items.desc: L bit set but the receiver cannot install the filter as an LPM route.
